claim: Acute hypoxia contributes to brain damage arising from stroke, heart attack, and head trauma.
source: Acute hypoxia contributes to brain damage arising from such common conditions as stroke, heart attack, and head trauma.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction without specific experimental data from this manuscript.

claim: In humans, decreased cerebral blood flow (ischemia) resulting in acute neuronal hypoxia correlates with pathological changes in electroencephalographic recordings and decreased electrical signaling in less than 150 s.
source: In humans, decreased cerebral blood flow (ischemia) resulting in acute neuronal hypoxia correlates with pathological changes in electroencephalographic recordings and decreased electrical signaling in less than 150 s (Sundt et al., 1981).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sundt et al., 1981.

claim: The first effect of hypoxia at the cellular level is to increase INa.
source: At the cellular level, the first effect of hypoxia is to increase INa (Boening et al., 1989; Stys et al., 1992)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Boening et al., 1989 and Stys et al., 1992.

claim: Inhibition of INa by tetrodotoxin (TTX) attenuates hypoxia-induced depolarization and reduces neuronal death in the hippocampus, hypothalamus, and neocortex.
source: inhibition of INa by tetrodotoxin (TTX) attenuates hypoxia-induced depolarization and reduces neuronal death in the hippocampus, hypothalamus, and neocortex (Boening et al., 1989; Stys et al., 1992; Weber and Taylor, 1994; Xie et al., 1994; Taylor et al., 1995; Fung et al., 1999; Horn and Waldrop, 2000; Raley-Susman et al., 2001; Banasiak et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The neuroprotective effects of TTX occur both independent of, and by reduction of the excitotoxic effects that follow INa-induced membrane depolarization.
source: Furthermore, the neuroprotective effects of TTX have been judged to occur both independent of, and by reduction of the excitotoxic effects that follow INa-induced membrane depolarization.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from prior literature.

claim: NaV1.2 is widely distributed in the brain.
source: Of the ten genes for α-subunits in mammals, four are predominant in the central nervous system including SCN2a, which encodes NaV1.2, an α-subunit that is widely distributed in the brain.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about NaV1.2 distribution.

claim: SCN2a mutations are associated with epilepsy and febrile seizures.
source: SCN2a mutations are associated with epilepsy and febrile seizures (Shi et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shi et al., 2012.

claim: Hypoxia increases INa in rat cerebellar granule neurons to a new stable level that is ~70% higher within 40 s.
source: When O2 was lowered from ambient levels to 5% by perfusion of cells with hypoxic solutions (Plant et al., 2002), the mean peak INa increased over 40 s to a new, stable level that was ~70% higher, −294 ± 25 pA/pF (Figure 1a and Table 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a and Table 1.

claim: Hypoxia did not alter the kinetics of recovery of INa from the fast-inactivated state.
source: Hypoxia did not alter the kinetics of recovery of INa from the fast-inactivated state (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: SUMO1 in the recording pipette increased CGN INa by ~76% and left-shifted V½ and SSI by −13 ± 1 mV and −10 ± 3 mV, respectively.
source: Here, seeking evidence for regulation of INa by the SUMO pathway, we delivered 100 pm SUMO1 into CGN via the patch-pipette, a concentration that produces maximal effects on the K+ channels. We observed SUMO-induced changes in INa like those produced by acute hypoxia: peak INa increased by ~76% and V½ and SSI were left-shifted by −13 ± 1 mV and −10 ± 3 mV, respectively (Figure 1c,d and Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c,d and Table 1.

claim: Intracellular application of 250 pm SENP1 deSUMOylase suppressed peak INa by ~75% to −42 ± 12 pA/pF and right-shifted V½ and SSI by 15 ± 1 mV and 14 ± 2 mV, respectively.
source: Indeed, intracellular application of 250 pm SENP1 deSUMOylase via the pipette suppressed peak INa by ~75% to −42 ± 12 pA/pF and right-shifted V½ and SSI by 15 ± 1 mV and 14 ± 2 mV, respectively (Figure 1c,d and Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c,d and Table 1.

claim: Currents increased by SUMO1 were not further augmented by hypoxia.
source: Providing additional evidence that hypoxia acted on INa via the SUMO pathway, currents increased by SUMO1 were not further augmented by hypoxia, nor did hypoxia overcome suppression of INa by SENP1 (Figure 1c,d and Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c,d and Supplementary file 1a.

claim: Hypoxia did not overcome suppression of INa by SENP1.
source: Providing additional evidence that hypoxia acted on INa via the SUMO pathway, currents increased by SUMO1 were not further augmented by hypoxia, nor did hypoxia overcome suppression of INa by SENP1 (Figure 1c,d and Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c,d and Supplementary file 1a.

claim: The full excursion in V½ between SUMOylating and deSUMOylating conditions was 26.5 ± 3.0 mV.
source: The full excursion in V½ between SUMOylating and deSUMOylating conditions was 26.5 ± 3.0 mV (Figure 1d and Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1d and Table 1.

claim: Maximal currents at 0 mV were not significantly different for CGN at 21% O2 with control, SUMO1, or SENP1 in the pipette or on acute exposure to 5% O2.
source: Supporting the notion that rapid changes in INa were due to shifts in the conductance-voltage (G-V) relationship, rather than changes in the number of channels on the surface passing current or unitary channel conductance, maximal currents at 0 mV, a voltage where G-V relationships were saturated under all test conditions (Figure 1b and d), were not significantly different for CGN at 21% O2 with the three pipette solutions (i.e. control, SUMO1, or SENP1) or on acute exposure to 5% O2 (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b, d and Table 1.

claim: 250 nm CnTX inhibited ~90% of INa at −20 mV in CGN.
source: In keeping with this expression pattern, 250 nm CnTX, a toxin that blocks NaV1.2 ~100-fold more effectively than NaV1.6 (Wilson et al., 2011), inhibited ~90% of INa at −20 mV in CGN (Figure 1e).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e and a citation to Wilson et al., 2011.

claim: When CGN were subjected to acute hypoxia or SUMO1 was applied in the pipette, CnTX still blocked over 90% of INa.
source: When CGN were subjected to acute hypoxia, or SUMO1 was applied in the pipette, CnTX still blocked over 90% of INa, indicating that NaV1.2 remained the primary contributor to Na+ current under these conditions (Figure 1f).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: The residual current after CnTX blockade was insensitive to acute hypoxia, SUMO1 and SENP1.
source: In contrast, the residual current after CnTX blockade was insensitive to acute hypoxia, SUMO1 and SENP1 (Figure 1g), suggesting that other NaV channels did not contribute significantly to the hypoxic response.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1g.

claim: 50 nm AnTTX inhibited ~10% of INa under control conditions and >90% of the current remaining after CnTX application.
source: Supporting the notion that most of the residual current is passed by NaV1.6, 50 nm 4,9 anhydro-tetrodotoxin (AnTTX), a toxin that blocks NaV1.6 ~150-fold more effectively than NaV1.2 (Rosker et al., 2007), inhibited ~10% of INa under control conditions and >90% of the current remaining after CnTX application (Figure 1e,f).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e,f and a citation to Rosker et al., 2007.

claim: With SENP1 in the pipette, the fraction of INa blocked by CnTX was decreased and suppression by AnTTX was increased.
source: Moreover, with SENP1 in the pipette, the fraction of INa blocked by CnTX was decreased and suppression by AnTTX was increased (Figure 1h), the expected response if deSUMOylation decreased the activity of NaV1.2 channels so that NaV1.6 channels passed a larger fraction of the current.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1h and logical inference.

claim: When combined, CnTX and AnTTX blocked >95% of INa in all CGN studied.
source: When combined, CnTX and AnTTX blocked >95% of INa in all CGN studied.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: In ambient O2, 7.8 ± 2.3% of NaV1.2 voxels showed FRET with SUMO1.
source: Thus, in ambient O2, 7.8 ± 2.3% of NaV1.2 voxels showed FRET (Figure 2a, n = 10 neurons)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: In neurons exposed to 1% O2 for 5 min, the percentage of voxels showing FRET increased ~4-fold to 29.6 ± 7.6%.
source: whereas in neurons exposed to 1% O2 for 5 min, the percentage of voxels showing FRET increased ~4-fold to 29.6 ± 7.6% (Figure 2b, n = 8 neurons).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: No FRET was observed between NaV1.2 and GAD67.
source: Supporting specificity of signals generated between NaV1.2 and SUMO1, no FRET was observed between NaV1.2 and GAD67, an abundant cytosolic protein (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Triple co-localization of SUMO1, NaV1.2, and biotin-labeled membrane proteins delineated the circumference of the neuronal soma.
source: Triple co-localization delineated the circumference of the neuronal soma (n = 5), consistent with plasma membrane localization of SUMOylated NaV1.2, as predicted by the electrophysiological studies.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d and inference from the data.

claim: In CGN cultured at 7% O2, decreasing O2 to 1.5% led to an acute increase in mean peak INa of ~65%.
source: Next, CGN cultured for 7–10 days at 7% O2 were evaluated at 7% O2 and then on exposure to 1.5% O2; the decrease in O2 led to an acute increase in mean peak INa of ~65% and, starting from a baseline for V½ of −42 ± 1.5 mV and −57 ± 3 mV, V½ and SSI were left-shifted by −8 ± 2 mV and −11 ± 3 mV, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: SUMO1 increased INa in CGN cultured at 7% O2 by ~68%, in association with left-shifts in V½ and SSI of − 8 ± 1.5 mV and −12 ± 3 mV, respectively.
source: Similarly, SUMO1 increased INa in CGN cultured at 7% O2 by ~68%, in association with left-shifts in V½ and SSI of − 8 ± 1.5 mV and −12 ± 3 mV, respectively
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: SENP1 suppressed INa in CGN cultured at 7% O2 by ~70% and right-shifted V½ and SSI by 9 ± 1 mV and 8 ± 2 mV, respectively.
source: while SENP1 suppressed INa by ~70% and right-shifted V½ and SSI by 9 ± 1 mV and 8 ± 2 mV, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Acute hypoxia altered the function of wild type NaV1.2 channels expressed in CHO cells in the same manner as seen for native INa in CGN.
source: Next, we observed that acute hypoxia altered the function of wild type NaV1.2 channels expressed in CHO cells in the same manner as seen for native INa in CGN (Figure 5a and Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5a and Table 1.

claim: NaV1.2 channels in CHO cells responded to acute hypoxia with an increase in mean peak current-density of ~70% in less than 40 s in association with leftward shifts in V½ and SSI of −11 ± 1 mV and −13 ± 2 mV, respectively.
source: Moreover, NaV1.2 channels responded to acute hypoxia with an increase in mean peak current-density of ~70% in less than 40 s in association with leftward shifts in V½ and SSI of −11 ± 1 mV and −13 ± 2 mV, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The total excursion in V½ for NaV1.2 channels in CHO cells between SUMOylation and deSUMOylation treatments was 27.5 ± 1.0 mV.
source: The total excursion in V½ for NaV1.2 channels in CHO cells between these treatments favoring SUMOylation and deSUMOylation was 27.5 ± 1.0 mV, as it was for CGN INa.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Expression of NaV1.2-Lys38Gln channels produced currents that were insensitive to acute hypoxia, SUMO1, and SENP1.
source: Supporting the essential role of SUMOylation of Lys38 in the hypoxic response, expression of NaV1.2-Lys38Gln channels produced currents that were insensitive to acute hypoxia, SUMO1, and SENP1 (Figure 5b and Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5b and Table 1.

claim: The β1 subunit did not appear to play a role in the hypoxic response of Nav1.2 via Lys38 or to the regulation of channel activity by the SUMO pathway.
source: Of note, the β1 subunit did not appear to play a role in the hypoxic response of Nav1.2 via Lys38 or to the regulation of channel activity by the SUMO pathway. Expression of the α subunits without β1 did not modify the responses of NaV1.2 channels to acute hypoxia, SUMO1, and SENP1 nor did it alter insensitivity of NaV1.2-Lys38Gln channels to the same three manipulations (Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Supplementary file 1c.

claim: Lys38 is in a sequence motif, Pro-Lys38-Gln-Glu, which is conserved near the N-terminus of NaV1.2 from zebrafish to humans.
source: Lys38 is in a sequence motif, Pro-Lys38-Gln-Glu (Figure 6a), which is conserved near the N-terminus of NaV1.2 from zebrafish to humans.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 6a.

claim: MS-MS sequencing identified a peak at the predicted size for a fragment carrying Lys38 linked via its side-chain to the Gly-Gly SUMO1 remnant.
source: The spectrum included a peak at the predicted size for a fragment carrying Lys38 linked via its side-chain to the Gly-Gly SUMO1 remnant, and MS-MS sequencing identified it uniquely to be the three-ended product (Figure 6c,d).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 6c,d.

claim: Acute hypoxia increased the fraction of CFP-NaV1.2 particles with mCherry-SUMO1 ~4-fold (from 20% to 80%).
source: Acute hypoxia increased the fraction of CFP-NaV1.2 particles with mCherry-SUMO1 ~4-fold (from 20% to 80%), as expected due to hypoxia-induced SUMOylation (Figure 7b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7b.

claim: SENP1 in the recording pipette suppressed both baseline and hypoxia-induced SUMOylation of CFP-NaV1.2 by mCherry-SUMO1 so that colocalized particles were decreased.
source: In contrast, SENP1 in the recording pipette suppressed both baseline and hypoxia-induced SUMOylation of CFP-NaV1.2 by mCherry-SUMO1 so that colocalized particles were decreased (Figure 7c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7c.

claim: Expression of CFP-NaV1.2-Lys38Gln and mCherry-SUMO1 rarely yielded colocalization of the fluorophores in both ambient O2 and hypoxic conditions.
source: Similarly, expression of CFP-NaV1.2-Lys38Gln and mCherry-SUMO1 rarely yielded colocalization of the fluorophores in both ambient O2 and hypoxic conditions (Figure 7d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7d.

claim: Observing only a single mCherry-SUMO1 in particles confirmed that only Lys38 on the α-subunit was SUMOylated, polySUMO1 chains were not formed, and the β1 subunit was not SUMOylated.
source: Because channels are formed with one NaV1.2 subunit, observing only a single mCherry-SUMO1 in particles as well confirmed three conclusions: only Lys38 on the α-subunit was SUMOylated; polySUMO1 chains were not formed; and, the β1 subunit was not SUMOylated.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the single bleaching step data.

claim: Acute hypoxia recruited mCherry-SUMO1 to the cell surface only at sites where CFP-NaV1.2 channels were already present and without altering the number of channels at the surface.
source: Supporting the conclusion that changes in O2 lead to rapid SUMOylation of NaV1.2, acute hypoxia recruited mCherry-SUMO1 to the cell surface only at sites where CFP-NaV1.2 channels were already present and without altering the number of channels at the surface (Figure 8a,b and Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8a,b and Table 2.

claim: After 2 min of hypoxia, an additional 50% of channel pixels were localized with mCherry-SUMO1, increasing the total to 65% (265 ± 12/µm2) with 35% unmodified by the tagged SUMO (137 ± 8/µm2).
source: After 2 min of hypoxia, an additional 50% of channel pixels were localized with mCherry-SUMO1, increasing the total to 65% (265 ± 12/µm2) with 35% unmodified by the tagged SUMO (137 ± 8/µm2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Although hypoxia increased the surface density of mCherry-SUMO1 associated with CFP-NaV1.2 by ~4-fold, there was no change in the level of CFP-NaV1.2 (407/µm2 versus 402/µm2).
source: Although hypoxia increased the surface density of mCherry-SUMO1 associated with CFP-NaV1.2 by ~4-fold, there was no change in the level of CFP-NaV1.2 (407/µm2 versus 402/µm2) and free mCherry-SUMO1 on the surface remained at low levels (4/µm2 versus 12/µm2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The time course for the increase in NaV1.2 channel current matched the rate of appearance of mCherry-SUMO1 at the plasma membrane with CFP-NaV1.2.
source: Consistent with a direct mechanism of action, the time course for the increase in NaV1.2 channel current matched the rate of appearance of mCherry-SUMO1 at the plasma membrane with CFP-NaV1.2 (Figure 8e and Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8e and Table 2.

claim: Under ambient conditions, mCherry-SUMO1 and CFP-NaV1.2 had a mean Manders' coefficient of co-localization of 0.22 and this increased to 0.72 over 40 s of hypoxia.
source: Under ambient conditions, mCherry-SUMO1 and CFP-NaV1.2 had a mean Manders' coefficient of co-localization of 0.22 and this increased to 0.72 over 40 s of hypoxia, showing a rate of rise of 17 ± 3% per 10 s.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Channels formed with CFP-NaV1.2 and mCherry-SUMO1 showed a time course for increased mean peak current-density of 15 ± 2% per 10 s (from −120 ± 8 pA/pF to −198 ± 10 pA/pF at −20 mV over 40 s, ~70% increase).
source: Similarly, channels formed with CFP-NaV1.2 and mCherry-SUMO1 showed a time course for increased mean peak current-density of 15 ± 2% per 10 s (from −120 ± 8 pA/pF to −198 ± 10 pA/pF at −20 mV over 40 s, ~70% increase).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The increase in surface levels mCherry-SUMO1 in response to acute hypoxia, and its co-localization with CFP-NaV1.2, were insensitive to 5 µm TTX.
source: Finally, we confirmed that hypoxia-induced SUMOylation of CFP-NaV1.2 in CHO cells was not triggered secondary to an increase in Na+ flux through the channels by showing that the increase in surface levels mCherry-SUMO1 in response to acute hypoxia, and its co-localization with CFP-NaV1.2, were insensitive to 5 µm TTX, a concentration that inhibited >95% of the Na+ current (Figure 8f).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8f.

claim: SUMOylation of NaV1.2 channels at the plasma membrane underlies the immediate increase in INa in response to acute hypoxia in cultured neurons and CHO cells.
source: Here, we show that SUMOylation of NaV1.2 channels at the plasma membrane underlies the immediate increase in INa in response to acute hypoxia in cultured neurons and CHO cells.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence throughout the manuscript.

claim: This is the first report to demonstrate rapid modulation of the SUMO pathway over just 10's of s.
source: In addition, while chronic stressors, including low tissue oxygenation, have been associated with global changes in SUMOylation, this is the first report, to our knowledge, to demonstrate rapid modulation of the SUMO pathway over just 10's of s.
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding in the context of existing literature.

claim: Hypoxia acts directly via SUMOylation of NaV1.2 Lys38.
source: Together, the following observations support the notion that hypoxia acts directly via SUMOylation of NaV1.2 Lys38: modification of Lys38 is demonstrated directly by FRET and MS (Figures 4 and 6); hypoxia does not alter the current passed by NaV1.2-Lys38Gln channels nor INa in neurons pretreated with SUMO1 (Figures 1 and 5); hypoxia cannot overcome suppression of INa by SENP1 (Figures 1 and 5); and, the time-course of SUMOylation of Lys38 matches the increase in NaV1.2 currents observed when CHO cells are subjected to hypoxia (Figure 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence from Figures 1, 4, 5, 6, and 8.

claim: Hypoxia-mediated SUMOylation of NaV1.2 is observed in the presence of TTX, showing that Na+ flux is not a prerequisite for channel SUMOylation.
source: That hypoxia-mediated SUMOylation of NaV1.2 is observed in the presence of TTX shows that Na+ flux is not a prerequisite for channel SUMOylation.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data showing TTX does not prevent SUMOylation.

claim: These findings offer a molecular rationale for acute, hypoxia-induced increases in the activity of neuronal NaV channels.
source: These findings offer a molecular rationale for acute, hypoxia-induced increases in the activity of neuronal NaV channels (Boening et al., 1989; Horn and Waldrop, 2000; Raley-Susman et al., 2001; Hammarström and Gage, 2000), a well-known trigger for the subsequent cascade of pathological events leading to cellular injury (Banasiak et al., 2004; Fung and Haddad, 1997).
evidence: This claim is based on the experimental findings of this study and citations to prior literature.

claim: NaV1.2 channels and SUMO pathway enzymes may be valuable therapeutic targets for reducing damage due to acute hypoxic insults to central neurons.
source: Our findings suggest that NaV1.2 channels and SUMO pathway enzymes may be valuable therapeutic targets for reducing damage due to acute hypoxic insults to central neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the findings of the study.

claim: CFP-NaV1.2 subunits and YFP-SUMO1 reach the cell surface when expressed together in CHO cells.
source: Both YFP-SUMO1 and CFP-NaV1.2 were visualized at the plasma membrane when expressed together in CHO cells (Figure 4a)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The time constant (τ) for donor photobleaching of CFP-NaV1.2 was prolonged from under 10 s to ~30 s when the channel was expressed with YFP-SUMO1.
source: Consistent with SUMOylation of CFP-NaV1.2, the time course of CFP decay with continuous illumination, as assessed by the time constant (τ) for donor photobleaching, was prolonged from under 10 s to ~30 s when the channel was expressed with YFP-SUMO1 (Figure 4b,c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b,c.

claim: CFP-NaV1.2 showed FRET with YFP-Ubc9.
source: CFP-NaV1.2 also showed FRET with YFP-Ubc9, the E2 SUMO-conjugating enzyme that binds to its targets only when the Lys residues subject to modification are present (Plant et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to Plant et al., 2011.

claim: FRET was not observed on expression of CFP-NaV1.2 with linkage-incompetent YFP-SUMO195 or soluble YFP.
source: In contrast, FRET was not observed on expression of CFP-NaV1.2 with linkage-incompetent YFP-SUMO195 (a variant that lacks the terminal Gly-Gly motif present in mature SUMO197) or soluble YFP; in both cases, τ was less than 10 s.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Mutating Lys38 to Gln produced CFP-NaV1.2-Lys38Gln subunits that reached the CHO cell surface like wild type CFP-NaV1.2.
source: Mutating Lys38 to Gln, removing the side chain subject to SUMO modification, produced CFP-NaV1.2-Lys38Gln subunits that reached the CHO cell surface like wild type CFP-NaV1.2.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: CFP-NaV1.2-Lys38Gln failed to exhibit FRET with either YFP-SUMO1 or YFP-Ubc9.
source: However, in contrast with CFP-NaV1.2, the mutant failed to exhibit FRET with either YFP-SUMO1 or YFP-Ubc9.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The absence of FRET supported the conclusion that Lys38 was required for SUMOylation of the NaV1.2 channel complex and suggested that no other Lys in the α subunit or the β1 subunit was subject to SUMOylation.
source: The absence of FRET supported the conclusion that Lys38 was required for SUMOylation of the NaV1.2 channel complex and suggested that no other Lys in the α subunit or the β1 subunit was subject to SUMOylation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the FRET data.

claim: Tagging NaV1.2 with CFP (CFP-NaV1.2) did not alter the biophysical properties of the channel nor its responsiveness to hypoxia, SUMO1, or SENP1.
source: Tagging NaV1.2 with CFP (CFP-NaV1.2) did not alter the biophysical properties of the channel nor its responsiveness to hypoxia, SUMO1, or SENP1 (Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Supplementary file 1a.

claim: Tagging the N-terminus of SUMO1 with FPs does not alter their operation with NaV1.2.
source: As we previously reported, tagging the N-terminus of SUMO1 with FPs does not alter their operation, and this was observed here with NaV1.2 (Rajan et al., 2005; Plant et al., 2010, 2011, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to prior work.

claim: In response to photobleaching, particles containing both CFP-NaV1.2 and mCherry-SUMO1 showed only a single bleaching step for each fluorophore under both normoxic and hypoxic conditions.
source: In response to photobleaching, these particles showed only a single bleaching step for each fluorophore under both normoxic and hypoxic conditions, indicating the presence of one fluorescent subunit of each type (Figure 7a,b and Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7a,b and Table 2.

claim: During 20 min of post-hypoxia recovery in ambient O2, the total number of CFP-NaV1.2 surface particles decreased by ~10% without a change in the fraction of channels localized with mCherry-SUMO1.
source: During 20 min of post-hypoxia recovery in ambient O2, the total number of CFP-NaV1.2 surface particles decreased by ~10% without a change in the fraction of channels localized with mCherry-SUMO1 (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Table 2.

claim: The decrease in fluorescent NaV1.2 particles on the surface was due to CFP photobleaching, consistent with the idea that neither acute hypoxia-induced SUMOylation nor re-oxygenation led to net addition or removal of CFP-NaV1.2 channels from the CHO cell plasma membrane.
source: Because current density decreased by just ~2% over the same period, we suspected that the decrease in fluorescent NaV1.2 particles on the surface was due to CFP photobleaching, in-keeping with the idea that neither acute hypoxia-induced SUMOylation nor re-oxygenation led to net addition or removal of CFP-NaV1.2 channels from the CHO cell plasma membrane; a conclusion supported as well by the similar size of CFP-NaV1.2 currents recorded at 0 mV in ambient O2 and 5% O2 (Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data shown in Supplementary file 1a.

claim: 100 nm SENP1 suppressed recruitment of mCherry-SUMO1 to the cell surface and abolished changes in peak current density, V½ and SSI in response to hypoxia.
source: Corroborating a role for SUMOylation of NaV1.2 in the response to hypoxia, 100 nm SENP1 suppressed recruitment of mCherry-SUMO1 to the cell surface (3 ± 2/ µm2), and abolished changes in peak current density, V½ and SSI in response to hypoxia (Figure 8c and Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8c and Table 2.

claim: Expression of CFP-NaV1.2-Lys38Gln channels eliminated recruitment of mCherry-SUMO1 to the cell surface and showed no changes in biophysical parameters in response to hypoxia.
source: Similarly, expression of CFP-NaV1.2-Lys38Gln channels (309 ± 12/ µm2) eliminated recruitment of mCherry-SUMO1 to the cell surface (4 ± 2/ µm2) and showed no changes in biophysical parameters in response to hypoxia (Figure 8d and Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8d and Table 2.

claim: Both the Manders' coefficient and current density were stable during 5 min of hypoxia and 10 min of subsequent recovery in ambient O2.
source: Both the Manders' coefficient and current density were stable during 5 min of hypoxia and 10 min of subsequent recovery in ambient O2.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Hypoxia-induced the SUMOylation of CFP-NaV1.2 channels by co-expressed mCherry-SUMO1 to a steady state of ~65–80% of the channels in <1 min in CHO cells.
source: Hypoxia-induced the SUMOylation of CFP-NaV1.2 channels by co-expressed mCherry-SUMO1 to a steady state of ~65–80% of the channels in <1 min in CHO cells (Figures 7 and 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: SUMOylation increases excitability by suppressing the activity of background K+ channels.
source: Previously, we demonstrated that SUMOylation increases excitability by suppressing the activity of background K+ channels (Rajan et al., 2005; Plant et al., 2010, 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: SUMOylation suppresses voltage-gated K+ channels that stabilize cells below firing threshold and restore cells to baseline after excitatory events.
source: and voltage-gated K+ channels (Plant et al., 2011) that stabilize cells below firing threshold and restore cells to baseline after excitatory events, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: SUMOylation augments the activity of voltage-gated NaV channels that initiate and propagate action potentials.
source: Now, we report that SUMOylation augments the activity of voltage-gated NaV channels that initiate and propagate action potentials, expanding the known targets through which the SUMO pathway can regulate neuronal activity.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: SUMO did not regulate hippocampal pyramidal cell INa, a current carried predominantly NaV1.1 and NaV1.6.
source: Of note, we found that SUMO did not regulate hippocampal pyramidal cell INa, a current carried predominantly NaV1.1 and NaV1.6 (Gong et al., 1999; Vacher et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to prior work.

claim: SUMO regulation of NaV channels may be isoform-specific.
source: This suggests that SUMO regulation of NaV channels may be isoform-specific, a notion supported by the failure of the small amount of INa in rat CGN that was not carried by NaV1.2 to respond to hypoxia, SUMO1 or SENP1, a current we attribute primarily to NaV1.6 based on its pharmacology.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data.

claim: NaV1.2 current remains elevated due to SUMOylation for at least 10–20 min following return to ambient O2 in both CGN and CHO cells.
source: Here, we observe that NaV1.2 current remains elevated due to SUMOylation for at least 10–20 min following return to ambient O2 in both CGN and CHO cells (Figures 1 and 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 5.

claim: An acute hypoxic challenge to hypothalamic neurons induced an increase in NaV current that recovered when the cells were returned to normoxia.
source: In contrast, an acute hypoxic challenge to hypothalamic neurons induced an increase in NaV current that recovered when the cells were returned to normoxia (Horn and Waldrop, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Horn and Waldrop, 2000.

claim: The baseline O2 level in mammalian brain tissue has been estimated to be as low as ~7% under normal, healthy conditions and to drop to under 2% with ischemia.
source: However, the baseline O2 level in mammalian brain tissue has been estimated to be as low as ~7% under normal, healthy conditions and to drop to under 2% with ischemia (Ponce et al., 2012; Lyons et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ponce et al., 2012 and Lyons et al., 2016.

claim: Rat CGN tolerate long-term culture in 7% O2.
source: First, rat CGN were confirmed to tolerate long-term culture in 7% O2, as we previously observed for rat hippocampal neurons (Shelat et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to Shelat et al., 2013.

claim: Medications offering broad neuroprotective efficacy in patients with brain hypoxia and ischemia are lacking.
source: Despite extensive discovery efforts, medications offering broad neuroprotective efficacy in patients with brain hypoxia and ischemia are lacking (Rogalewski et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rogalewski et al., 2006.
